triage.name: Prostate Cancer
triage.reason: Common malignancy presenting with urinary symptoms or abnormal screening; diagnosis reachable via history, exam, PSA and biopsy.

review_issues: auto-repaired: labs: dropped 'psa' (not in the reference table)

demographics: Most common non-skin cancer in men in the US
Black men have higher incidence and are more likely to present at a younger age and with more advanced disease
Men with a first-degree relative with prostate cancer are at higher risk

risk_factors.text: Family history of prostate cancer in a father or brother
Inherited mutations such as BRCA1/BRCA2 or Lynch syndrome

family_history: Prostate cancer in a father or brother
Breast or ovarian cancer in a female relative suggesting BRCA mutation
Colorectal or other Lynch syndrome-associated cancers

chief_complaints.text: I have to get up several times a night to pee
My urine stream is weak and it takes a while to start
My doctor said my PSA blood test was high
I have a dull ache in my lower back and hips that won't go away
I saw blood in my urine

hpi.onset: Insidious; often no symptoms at all and detected only by an abnormal PSA or digital rectal exam
hpi.duration: Weeks to months of urinary symptoms; screening-detected cases are asymptomatic
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive urinary symptoms; locally advanced or metastatic disease may add bone pain, weight loss or blood in urine or semen
hpi.location: Pelvis, with urinary symptoms referred to the bladder outlet; metastatic pain in lower back, hips or pelvis
hpi.radiation: Bone pain may radiate to the back, hips or thighs when there is metastatic spread
hpi.quality: Obstructive and irritative urinary symptoms; bone pain is dull and constant
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate for early disease; severe when there is urinary retention or metastatic bone pain
hpi.timing: Nocturia and hesitancy are worse at night and with a full bladder; bone pain is constant and worse at night

associated_symptoms.text: Hesitancy and straining to start urination
Persistent lower back, hip or pelvic pain

pertinent_negatives: Gross hematuria with clots throughout the stream

negatives: Erectile dysfunction as an isolated complaint

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with metastatic disease such as bone pain, pathologic fracture or spinal cord compression, or may have no urinary symptoms at all.
Obesity is associated with more aggressive disease and higher risk of biochemical recurrence; digital rectal exam may be less reliable.
Lower urinary tract symptoms may be attributed to diabetic neuropathy or medications rather than prostate disease, delaying diagnosis.
missing_classic_features: Clear temporal relationship of symptoms to prostate enlargement

general.moderate: Well-appearing but uncomfortable; may shift in the chair due to pelvic or back discomfort
general.severe: Ill-appearing, fatigued, may have visible weight loss or use a cane for bone pain
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, diaphoretic, in severe pain or with neurologic deficits from cord compression

findings.maneuver: Perform a digital rectal exam with a lubricated gloved finger, palpating the posterior surface of the prostate for nodules, asymmetry, or induration
findings.finding: Hard, irregular, or asymmetric nodule or area of induration on the prostate

findings.maneuver: Assess prostate size and consistency on digital rectal exam
findings.finding: Enlarged, smooth, rubbery prostate without nodules (consistent with BPH rather than cancer)
Normal-sized, smooth, non-tender prostate without nodules or induration

findings.maneuver: Palpate the prostate on digital rectal exam
findings.finding: Firm, tender, boggy prostate (suggests prostatitis rather than cancer)
Suprapubic tenderness or palpable bladder (suggests urinary retention)

findings.maneuver: Palpate the pelvis, hips, and lower back; apply gentle pressure over the sacrum and iliac crests
findings.finding: Focal bony tenderness over the pelvis, hips, or lower back (suggests metastatic bone involvement)

findings.maneuver: Palpate the ribs and long bones
findings.finding: Focal bony tenderness over the ribs or long bones (suggests metastatic bone involvement)

findings.maneuver: Press over the pretibial area and dorsum of the foot
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the lower extremities (may suggest pelvic lymph node obstruction or venous stasis)

findings.maneuver: Palpate the inguinal, supraclavicular, and cervical lymph node chains
findings.finding: Enlarged, firm lymph nodes (suggests metastatic spread)

findings.maneuver: Test lower extremity strength, sensation, and deep tendon reflexes; assess gait
findings.finding: Weakness, sensory loss, or hyperreflexia in the lower extremities (suggests spinal cord compression from metastasis)

findings.maneuver: Palpate both testes and scrotal contents

labs.caveat: Elevated alkaline phosphatase suggests bone metastases or liver involvement; confirm the source with fractionation or imaging.
Hypercalcemia suggests osteolytic bone metastases; correct for albumin.
Anemia of chronic disease or bone marrow involvement; may also reflect hematuria.
Elevated creatinine suggests obstructive uropathy from locally advanced disease or dehydration; check for hydronephrosis.
Microscopic hematuria may be the only urinary finding; also seen in BPH, infection, and stones.
Mild sterile pyuria can accompany prostate cancer or obstruction; marked pyuria with positive nitrite suggests infection instead.

findings.text: Hypoechoic lesion in the peripheral zone

imaging.preferred_when: Before biopsy to target lesions and assess extraprostatic extension

findings.text: Focal lesion in the peripheral zone with restricted diffusion and early enhancement (PI-RADS 4–5)
Extraprostatic extension or seminal vesicle invasion
Multiple focal areas of increased uptake in the axial skeleton (osteoblastic metastases)

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Staging for nodal or visceral metastases

findings.text: Enlarged pelvic or retroperitoneal lymph nodes
Focal uptake in the prostate bed or lymph nodes
Skeletal uptake corresponding to bone metastases

Baseline before biopsy or treatment; may show anemia
Assesses renal function and calcium before imaging or treatment
Evaluates hematuria and excludes urinary infection

initial.only_if: PSA is elevated or DRE is abnormal and biopsy is planned

confirmatory.why: Tissue diagnosis and Gleason grade; the only way to confirm prostate cancer

supporting.why: Targets biopsy and assesses local extent
supporting.only_if: prior biopsy is negative but suspicion remains, or to target lesions before first biopsy
high-risk disease (PSA >20 ng/mL, high Gleason grade) or bone pain

supporting.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

supporting.why: More sensitive staging and recurrence localization

supporting.only_if: neurologic deficits or severe back pain suggest spinal cord compression
bone pain, fatigue, or high-risk disease

not_indicated.why: Not a routine staging study; CT or PSMA PET is preferred when staging is needed
No role in prostate cancer evaluation
Not indicated unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis

decision_points: Discuss benefits and harms of PSA screening; do not screen without shared decision-making
Confirm abnormal PSA with a repeat test before biopsy, and treat any urinary infection first
Use risk calculators and MRI to decide whether to biopsy
Stage with bone scan or PSMA PET only in high-risk disease or when symptoms suggest metastases
Suspect spinal cord compression in any patient with prostate cancer and new back pain or neurologic deficits; image urgently

criteria.name: Gleason grading / Grade Group
criteria.summary: Prostate biopsy tissue is assigned a Gleason score based on the two most common patterns (1–5 each); the sum ranges from 6 to 10. Grade Group 1 = Gleason 6, Group 2 = 3+4=7, Group 3 = 4+3=7, Group 4 = 8, Group 5 = 9–10. Higher groups indicate more aggressive cancer.

criteria.name: D'Amico risk stratification
criteria.summary: Localized prostate cancer is classified as low, intermediate, or high risk using PSA level, Gleason score, and clinical T stage. Low risk: PSA <10 ng/mL, Gleason ≤6, T1–T2a. Intermediate: PSA 10–20, Gleason 7, or T2b. High: PSA >20, Gleason 8–10, or T2c–T3.

differential.name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
differential.why_considered: The most common cause of lower urinary tract symptoms in older men and the main reason for an elevated PSA that is not cancer

history: Gradual onset of nocturia, hesitancy and weak stream over years
No bone pain, weight loss or hematuria
Symptoms fluctuate with fluid intake and medications
exam: Smooth, rubbery, symmetrically enlarged prostate without nodules or induration
labs: PSA usually mildly elevated and stable over time
imaging: Enlarged prostate with uniform echotexture and no suspicious peripheral-zone lesion
No uptake on bone scan or PSMA PET

differential.name: Acute bacterial prostatitis
differential.why_considered: Causes urinary symptoms, an elevated PSA and a tender prostate, and can mimic cancer on presentation
differential.trigger: Fever, chills, dysuria and a tender boggy prostate

history: Acute onset over hours to days
exam: Suprapubic tenderness; may have systemic toxicity
labs: Marked pyuria and positive urine culture
PSA elevated acutely and falls after treatment
imaging: No focal peripheral-zone lesion on MRI
Ultrasound may show heterogeneous prostate or abscess

differential.name: Urinary tract infection
differential.why_considered: Shares dysuria, frequency, urgency and hematuria with prostate cancer and can raise PSA

history: Nocturia less prominent than in prostate enlargement
No bone pain or weight loss
labs: Positive nitrite and leukocyte esterase with positive culture
PSA normal or only transiently elevated

differential.name: Nephrolithiasis
differential.why_considered: Can cause hematuria and flank or pelvic pain that may be mistaken for metastatic bone pain

history: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
Nausea and vomiting with the pain
exam: Prostate normal on digital rectal exam
imaging: No prostate lesion or bone metastases

differential.name: Metastatic bone disease from another primary
differential.why_considered: Osteoblastic bone lesions and bone pain in an older man can be mistaken for metastatic prostate cancer
differential.trigger: Bone pain with lytic or mixed lesions and a normal or only mildly elevated PSA

history: Known lung, breast, kidney or thyroid cancer
Weight loss, fatigue and night sweats
labs: Tumor markers may point to another primary
imaging: Lytic or mixed lesions rather than purely osteoblastic
Biopsy of bone lesion shows the other primary

differential.name: Testicular cancer
differential.why_considered: A young man with a testicular mass and elevated tumor markers can be confused with prostate disease, and both are genitourinary malignancies

severity.mild: Localized, low-risk disease: PSA <10 ng/mL, Gleason 6, clinical stage T1–T2a; often asymptomatic and detected by screening
severity.moderate: Localized intermediate-risk disease: PSA 10–20 ng/mL, Gleason 7, or T2b; lower urinary tract symptoms may be present but no metastases
severity.severe: Locally advanced or high-risk disease: PSA >20 ng/mL, Gleason 8–10, T2c–T3, or regional lymph node involvement; may have obstructive urinary symptoms or bone pain
severity.critical: Metastatic castration-resistant disease with spinal cord compression, pathologic fracture, hypercalcemia or visceral crisis

red_flags.finding: New back pain with lower extremity weakness, sensory loss or bowel/bladder dysfunction
red_flags.meaning: Spinal cord compression from vertebral metastasis; needs urgent MRI and steroids
Bone metastasis with cortical destruction; needs orthopedic evaluation
Bladder outlet obstruction from locally advanced disease; needs catheterization and urology evaluation

red_flags.finding: Gross hematuria with clots or falling hemoglobin
red_flags.meaning: Significant bleeding from prostate or bladder involvement; needs urology evaluation
Hypercalcemia of malignancy; check calcium and treat urgently

red_flags.finding: PSA doubling time under 6 months or rapidly rising PSA on androgen deprivation
red_flags.meaning: Castration-resistant progression; needs systemic therapy change

complications.name: Treatment-related erectile dysfunction and urinary incontinence
clues: Onset after radical prostatectomy or radiation

special_populations.differences: More likely to present with metastatic disease or with symptoms attributed to BPH; competing comorbidities make active surveillance and less aggressive treatment more appropriate.
Associated with more aggressive disease and higher risk of biochemical recurrence; digital rectal exam may be less reliable.
Lower urinary tract symptoms may be attributed to diabetic neuropathy or medications, delaying diagnosis; glycemic control affects treatment tolerance.
Obstructive uropathy from locally advanced disease can cause renal failure; adjust imaging contrast and systemic therapy dosing accordingly.

cancer.screening: The USPSTF recommends against routine PSA-based screening without shared decision-making. For men aged 55 to 69, screening should be an individual decision after discussing benefits and harms. For men 70 and older, screening is not recommended. Black men and men with a family history are at higher risk and may reasonably start the discussion earlier.
cancer.pathology: Adenocarcinoma accounts for the vast majority of prostate cancers and arises in the peripheral zone. Less common types include ductal, mucinous, neuroendocrine and small cell variants, and transitional cell carcinoma. Gleason grading assigns the two most common architectural patterns (1–5 each) and sums them to a score of 6 to 10; Grade Group 1 = Gleason 6, Group 2 = 3+4=7, Group 3 = 4+3=7, Group 4 = 8, Group 5 = 9–10.
cancer.staging_concepts: Staging uses the TNM system. T stage describes local extent from T1 (not palpable) through T2 (confined to prostate), T3 (extraprostatic extension or seminal vesicle invasion) and T4 (invasion of bladder, rectum or pelvic wall). N stage describes regional lymph nodes and M stage describes distant metastases. Risk groups combine PSA, Gleason score and clinical T stage: low risk is PSA <10 ng/mL, Gleason ≤6 and T1–T2a; intermediate is PSA 10–20, Gleason 7 or T2b; high is PSA >20, Gleason 8–10 or T2c–T3.
metastatic_sites: Bones, especially the axial skeleton (vertebrae, pelvis, ribs, femur)

key_questions.question: What urinary symptoms have you noticed, and when did they start?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset of nocturia, weak stream, hesitancy, urgency and frequency over weeks to months; symptoms of bladder outlet obstruction

key_questions.question: Have you had any blood in your urine or semen?
key_questions.looking_for: Hematuria or hematospermia, which raises concern for prostate or bladder involvement

key_questions.question: Do you have any pain in your lower back, hips or pelvis that does not go away?
key_questions.looking_for: Persistent dull bone pain suggesting metastatic spread to the axial skeleton

key_questions.question: Have you had any unintentional weight loss, fatigue or loss of appetite?
key_questions.looking_for: Constitutional symptoms suggesting advanced or metastatic disease

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, chills or burning with urination?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in prostate cancer; present suggests prostatitis or urinary tract infection

key_questions.question: Have you had a PSA test or a digital rectal exam, and what were the results?
key_questions.looking_for: Elevated PSA or an abnormal prostate exam that prompted the visit; prior values and trend over time

key_questions.question: Have you been diagnosed with an enlarged prostate or taken medication for it?
key_questions.looking_for: History of benign prostatic hyperplasia, which is the main look-alike and can also coexist

key_questions.question: Has a parent, sibling or child had prostate cancer?
key_questions.looking_for: First-degree relative with prostate cancer, which substantially increases risk

key_questions.question: Is there any history of breast, ovarian or colorectal cancer in your family?
key_questions.looking_for: BRCA mutation or Lynch syndrome, which raise prostate cancer risk

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, and how much alcohol or caffeine do you drink?
key_questions.looking_for: Smoking and caffeine or alcohol intake that worsen urinary symptoms and affect overall risk

key_questions.question: Have you had any trouble getting or keeping an erection, or pain with ejaculation?
key_questions.looking_for: Painful ejaculation or erectile dysfunction; baseline sexual function matters for treatment decisions

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a urinary catheter, prostate biopsy or other urinary procedure?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent instrumentation, which raises concern for infection rather than cancer

key_questions.question: Have you had any weakness, numbness or trouble controlling your bladder or bowels?
key_questions.looking_for: Neurologic deficits suggesting spinal cord compression from vertebral metastasis; requires urgent imaging

reasoning_points: Older man with gradual lower urinary tract symptoms or an asymptomatic elevated PSA
Risk factors including age over 50, Black race, and a first-degree relative with prostate cancer
Digital rectal exam showing a hard, irregular or asymmetric nodule or area of induration
Elevated PSA that is confirmed on repeat testing after treating any urinary infection
Persistent lower back, hip or pelvic pain suggesting bone metastases
Prostate biopsy showing adenocarcinoma with Gleason grading and Grade Group
Benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis and urinary tract infection considered and excluded
Spinal cord compression and hypercalcemia of malignancy screened for when symptoms suggest advanced disease

easy: Man over 60 with nocturia, weak stream and hesitancy
Hard, nodular prostate on digital rectal exam
medium: Asymptomatic man with an isolated elevated PSA and a normal digital rectal exam
Symptoms attributed to benign prostatic hyperplasia with a mildly elevated PSA
Man with lower back pain and a normal urinary history
Black man presenting at a younger age with more advanced disease
hard: Man with acute prostatitis and a transiently elevated PSA that normalizes after treatment
Older adult with bone pain and lytic lesions from another primary cancer
Patient with a negative biopsy but persistently rising PSA requiring MRI-targeted rebiopsy
Man presenting with spinal cord compression or pathologic fracture as the first sign
Lower urinary tract symptoms explained by diabetic neuropathy or medications rather than prostate disease
